_readme: This is the quality ceiling for the Theory reference, and it is a valid staging file. It lives OUTSIDE staging-theory/content/, so the merge glob never picks it up and the coverage test (DESIGN-THEORY.md C1) never counts its area_ids.
It contains three COMPLETE articles, one per hard case: a foundation article that assumes no grammar vocabulary at all; a heavy paradigm article; and a heavy contrast article.

The ids th_tm_01, th_tm_02 and th_tm_03 are RESERVED. The chapter authors write th_what_a_sentence_is, th_passive_forms and th_pp_vs_past_simple themselves and must not reuse a single sentence from this file. Copy the SHAPE, never the prose.
sequence_index and area_ids below are the REAL values of the articles being modelled, so you can see how they are derived. They are not claims on those slots.
Read DESIGN-THEORY.md sections 2 (schema), 5 (the writing standard) and 6 (the quantity targets) alongside this file.

_authoring_notes: THREE PLACES WHERE READING DESIGN-THEORY.md 2.4 ALONE WOULD MISLEAD YOU. All three are resolved in this file the way the contract as a whole requires.

1. The exceptions block illustrated in 2.4.13 is present-perfect content, but 2.5 does not give kind: comparison a part 7. Exceptions belong in th_present_perfect, not in the comparison article. th_tm_03 therefore ships no exceptions block.

2. The article_json example in 2.2 shows terms_introduced containing 'past participle'. The 4.3 ledger introduces the third form in th_five_verb_forms, earlier in the same chapter. A comparison article this late introduces no terms at all. th_tm_03 ships terms_introduced: [].

3. 2.5 gives kind: paradigm parts 2, 3 and 11 only, with no term_intro. The 4.3 ledger nonetheless names th_passive_forms as the sole introducer of 'agent'. The ledger wins: 6.2 permits a term_intro in an article of any kind whose ledger position demands one.

ONE GRAMMAR JUDGEMENT WORTH COPYING. th_tm_01 teaches that every English sentence needs a subject and a verb. That is the right default and it is what a learner should write. Instructions are the one systematic exception, and the article states it inside the rule rather than hiding it behind 'generally'. A rule with a named exception is still a rule; a rule with a hedge is not.

article_json.also_called: The subject, the verb, and the simple sentence
article_json.one_line: This lets you tell whether a group of words is a finished English sentence or only a piece of one.
article_json.short_answer: Every English sentence needs two things: who or what it is about, and a word that says what happens. *The bridge closed.*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: When is a group of words a real sentence, and when is it only half of one?

body.text: What every English sentence has to have
You can put ten words together and still not have a sentence. English asks for two things, and it asks for them every time. This article shows you what they are and how to check.

body.gloss: a group of words that says something complete

show_first.text: The lift is out of order.
show_first.mark: The lift is out of order.

show_first.text: The Norland depot closed in March.
show_first.mark: The Norland depot closed in March.

body.anchor_line: Each one stands on its own. You could say it to somebody who had heard nothing else, and they would understand it.

body.gloss: the word that says what happens or what is

show_first.text: The Ashfield clinic opens at eight.
Heavy rain closed the coast road.

body.anchor_line: Take it out and nothing is left but a list of things. Every sentence you have ever read in English has one.

body.gloss: who or what the sentence is about — it comes before the verb

show_first.text: The Sandmouth library opens at nine.

body.anchor_line: Some languages let you leave it out, because the ending of the verb already says who. English does not.

body.text: Seeing the two parts

body.lead_in: In each one, the first marked part says who or what, and the second says what happens.

items.text: The Marlow road flooded again on Tuesday.
items.gloss: A road went under water. That is the whole event.

items.text: Two lorries blocked the Sandmouth junction.
items.gloss: Two lorries stopped the traffic getting through.

items.text: My sister studies engineering at Brackenfield.
items.gloss: She is a student there at the moment.
It is too late to apply now.

body.so_what: Every one of them has a part that says who or what, and a part that says what happens.

body.caption: Two boxes. Fill both, and you have a sentence.

body.text: The rule, and how short a sentence can be
Every English sentence needs a subject and a verb. In an instruction the subject is *you*, and English leaves it out.

body.lead_in: These are as short as an English sentence gets. Nothing is missing from any of them.

items.gloss: Rain fell. That is everything the sentence says.
The site is not open any more.

body.so_what: Two parts are enough. A much longer group of words with only one of them is still not a sentence.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The new footbridge over the canal at Verdon.
body.right: The new footbridge over the canal at Verdon opened in March.
body.why_it_happens: The group of words is long and it names something clearly, so it feels finished. Nothing in it says what happened, so it is not a sentence yet.
body.smallest_fix: Add a word that says what happens: *opened*, *closed*, *is*.

body.wrong: The depot moved to Norland the journey now takes forty minutes.
body.right: The depot moved to Norland. The journey now takes forty minutes.
body.why_it_happens: The two parts are about one thing, so they feel like one sentence. Each part has its own subject and its own verb, so each one needs its own full stop.
body.smallest_fix: Count the words that say what happens. Two of those means two sentences.

body.heard: A sentence is a group of words that expresses a complete thought.
also_known_as: a sentence is one complete idea
body.truth: That describes a sentence. It does not let you check one. *The long queue outside the clinic* feels like a complete thought, and it is not a sentence, because nothing in it says what happened.
body.what_to_do: Do not ask whether it feels finished. Look for the two parts: who or what, and what happens.

body.heard: Every English sentence must have a subject written in it.
also_known_as: a sentence with no subject is always wrong
body.truth: It is the right default, and it is what you should write. Instructions are the one place English leaves the subject out. *Close the gate.* means *you close the gate*, and the *you* is understood.
body.what_to_do: Check that every sentence you write has a subject. The only ones that do not need a written subject are instructions.

body.mechanism: Spanish marks who is doing something on the end of the verb, so no separate subject word is needed.
body.right: It is raining again in Sandmouth.
body.fix: Put a subject word in, even when the verb already tells you who.

body.mechanism: Tamil links a subject to a description with no separate word for *is*. The description itself carries the marking.
body.right: The Sandmouth library is very old.
body.fix: Put *is*, *am* or *are* in, even when the sentence feels finished without it.

body.headline: Two parts. Who or what, and what happens.
points: Every English sentence needs a subject and a verb.
A long group of words with no verb in it is not a sentence.
Two words each saying what happens means two sentences, not one.
*It rained.* is a complete English sentence.

body.note: Answers are shown. Nothing here is recorded and nothing is marked.

items.prompt: Is this a sentence? *The two new benches by the Verdon canal.*
items.why: Nothing in it says what happens. Add a verb: *…were installed last month.*
*Snow* says who or what. *Fell* says what happens. Two parts is enough.

articles.title: Building the passive in every tense

article_json.also_called: Passive formation: *be* + past participle, and the *by*-agent
article_json.one_line: This lets you build a passive in any tense, so a sentence can start with the thing that was done to.
article_json.short_answer: Put the right form of *be* in front of the third form. *is painted*, *was painted*, *has been painted*, *will be painted*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I build a passive sentence at each different time?

body.text: How the passive is built, whatever the time
A passive always has two parts. A form of *be* carries the time and matches the subject. The third form of the main verb sits behind it and never changes.
So the only thing you choose is which form of *be* to use. The table below has all of them in one place, and you can come back to it.

body.caption: Only *be* changes. The third form stays the same in every row.
body.form_line: a form of *be* + the third form of the main verb

rows.note: *it's been* is *it has been* here. *been* is the clue.
*it'd been* is *it had been*, not *it would been*.

cells: it will not have been painted

rows.note: English does not use this one. The note under the table says why.

sub_tables.caption: The second word is the third form, not the past form.
A modal never changes shape. Put *be* or *have been* after it.
Keep the *by* part only when the doer is news.
rows: The hall was painted last week.
The hall was painted by the tenants.
The route was chosen by a panel of teachers.

gaps.note: *was* and *were* have no short form. Only *not* contracts here: *wasn't*, *weren't*.
Same reason. *was* does not run together with what comes before it.

gaps.cell: duration up to now, every column
gaps.note: This one would need *been being*. English does not use it. Say *it has been painted*, or put the sentence back in the active.

examples.text: The Verdon community hall is painted every spring.
examples.gloss: It happens every year. Who does it is not the point.

examples.text: The hall is being painted this week.
examples.gloss: The work is going on now and it is not finished.

examples.text: The report has been written by two of the tenants.
examples.gloss: The report exists now, and it says who wrote it.

examples.text: The fence had been painted before the inspection.
examples.gloss: The painting finished first. The inspection came after it.

examples.text: It'll be painted before the school reopens.
examples.gloss: The painting will happen at some point before then.

examples.text: The Marlow gates must be painted before winter.
examples.gloss: Somebody has to do it. The rule does not say who.

notes: *it's been painted* is *it has been painted*. The word after it tells you which one you are hearing.
Only two of the in-progress passives are in use: *is being painted* and *was being painted*.
The second word is always the third form. Never *it was wrote*.

body.caption: The passive moves the thing done to into the first slot.

body.text: Naming the doer with *by*

body.gloss: the doer, when a passive sentence names it after *by*

show_first.text: The canal path was cleared by three volunteers.
The design was chosen by a panel of teachers.
The bridge was rebuilt by the county council.

body.anchor_line: Most passive sentences have no agent at all, because most of the time nobody needs to know who did it.

body.text: Leave the agent out unless it is news. *The hall was painted last week* is a complete sentence and nobody is missing from it. Put *by* in when who did it is the point you are making.

body.lead_in: The same event, with and without the doer. Watch what the *by* part adds.

items.text: The old signal box was repainted last weekend.
items.gloss: The signal box looks new now. Who did the work is not the point.

items.text: The old signal box was repainted by the rail volunteers.
items.gloss: It looks new, and the point is that volunteers did it.

items.text: Two hundred trees were planted along the ring road.
items.gloss: The trees are there now. Nobody needs to know who dug the holes.

items.text: The whole scheme was funded by a single donation.
items.gloss: The money came from one gift, and that is the surprising part.

items.text: The whole thing was organised by two of the neighbours.
items.gloss: Two neighbours did all the organising, and that is worth saying.

body.so_what: Adding *by* changes what the sentence is about. Leave it out and the sentence is about the thing, not the doer.

body.text: Where the passive has no form at all

English avoids two forms of *be* side by side. That is why *been being* and *be being* do not appear, and why four combinations have no passive in normal use. When you need one of them, put the sentence back in the active.

body.headline: Pick the form of *be*. The third form never moves.

table.caption: One row per time. Only *be* changes.
rows: the hall is painted every spring

article_json.false_rule_absent_reason: The false rules about the passive are all about when to use it, not how to build it. They are named and killed in th_when_to_choose_the_passive, which owns that decision.

articles.title: Is the time you mean finished, or still open?

article_json.one_line: This lets you choose between two past forms that are both correct English, so the sentence says what you actually mean.
article_json.short_answer: Ask whether the stretch of time is finished. Finished: past simple, *closed in 2019*. Still open: present perfect, *has closed since 2019*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I choose between *I did* and *I have done*?

body.text: What you are actually choosing between

Both of these are correct English: *the panel met on Tuesday*, and *the panel has met twice this month*. Neither one is more polite or more advanced than the other. They say different things about time, and a reader hears the difference.

So what you are choosing is not a form. It is whether the stretch of time you have in mind is closed or still running. Get that wrong and the sentence is correct English, and says something you did not mean.
Is the time period finished, or still running?

body.question: Is the stretch of time I am talking about finished?

options.label: past simple
options.use_it_when: The stretch is finished, and it is usually named: *last month*, *in 2019*, *when I was a student*.
options.example: Applications closed at the end of March.

options.label: present perfect
options.use_it_when: The stretch runs up to now — *since*, *so far*, *this year* — or you name no time at all.
options.example: Applications have closed twice since the scheme began.

a.text: She taught at the Ashfield school for eleven years.
a.means: She does not teach there now. Those eleven years are over.

b.text: She has taught at the Ashfield school for eleven years.
b.means: She still teaches there. The eleven years are still running.

a.means: It happened, at some point that is now over. You are telling the story.

b.text: The council has closed two libraries.
b.means: Two libraries are shut. That is where things stand today.

a.text: Did you speak to the site manager?
a.means: You are asking about one occasion you both have in mind.

b.text: Have you spoken to the site manager?
b.means: You are asking whether it has happened at all yet.

minimal_pairs.only_difference: Did you speak / Have you spoken

a.means: In the time it stood, nobody repaired it. That time is over.

b.text: The footbridge has never been repaired.
b.means: It is still there, and nobody has repaired it yet.

body.deciding_factor: Find the time expression. If you can put a full stop after it and it still means a closed time, the verb is past simple.
body.trap: You were taught that the present perfect is the experience tense, so you reach for it whenever the sentence is about experience — which is most of the time.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. The choice pays in Speaking Part 1, in Task 1 where the end date is open, and in Task 2 background sentences.

body.intro: Three questions, in this order. Stop at the first one that answers.

steps.ask: Is there a time expression in the sentence?
Can you put a full stop after it and still mean a closed time?

verdict.why: A closed time and the present perfect cannot share a clause.

verdict.example: The line has closed twice since 2015.
verdict.why: The stretch is still running, so the verb stays open too.

steps.ask: Are you and your reader thinking of one particular occasion?

verdict.example: The surveyors found damp in both walls.
verdict.why: You are reporting one occasion that is over, so the verb is past simple.

branches.answer: No — you mean where things stand

verdict.example: The surveyors have found damp in both walls.
verdict.why: You are reporting the situation now, so the verb links back to now.

body.text: The three questions work in the order given. Most sentences stop at the second one, because most sentences that need this decision have a time expression somewhere in them.
The two forms, side by side

body.caption: *Have* plus the third form, against the plain past form.
rows: the past form on its own
footnotes: The third form is *painted*, *written*, *met*. All five shapes of a verb are in [th_five_verb_forms].

body.lead_in: The same event, with the time expression changed. Nothing else moves.

items.gloss: It shut that year. The year is over.

items.text: The depot has closed twice since 2015.
items.gloss: It shut twice, and the stretch from 2015 runs up to today.
Last week is finished, so the verb is finished too.

items.text: The depot has closed this week.
items.gloss: This week is still running, and the closure counts inside it.

body.so_what: Only the time expression changed, and it dragged the verb with it every time.

body.caption: *Since 2015* opens a stretch that is still running now.

body.text: Use the present perfect when the period of time you are talking about is still open, or when you name no time at all.

body.lead_in: No time expression in any of these. The verb is doing the work on its own.

items.text: The lift has broken down again.
items.gloss: It is broken now, and that is the problem.

items.text: The committee has agreed the new route.
items.gloss: The route is agreed. That is where things stand.

items.text: Two of the surveyors have resigned.
items.gloss: They are gone, and the team is two people short.

body.so_what: None of them names a time. Each one is about how things stand at the moment of speaking.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The council has approved the plan in 2019.
body.right: The council approved the plan in 2019.
body.why_it_happens: You are thinking about the result — the plan is still approved — so you reach for the form that links back to now. *In 2019* closes the stretch, and a closed stretch takes the past simple.
body.smallest_fix: Take the time expression out, or change *has approved* to *approved*.

body.wrong: Since 2015 the number of applicants dropped by a third.
body.right: Since 2015 the number of applicants has dropped by a third.
body.why_it_happens: *Since* looks like a past-time word, so the past form feels right. *Since* opens a stretch that runs up to now, and a verb inside that stretch has to stay open too.
body.smallest_fix: Change *dropped* to *has dropped*. The stretch from 2015 is still running.

option_a.label: British English
option_a.example: The panel has just published the figures.

option_b.label: American English
option_b.example: The panel just published the figures.

body.why_this_default: The perfect version is accepted everywhere and never sounds wrong. This is a house choice for our examples, not a rule of English.

body.heard: If the sentence has *already*, *yet* or *just* in it, you must use the present perfect.
body.truth: Those words often turn up with it. They do not decide it — the stretch of time does. *I have visited Verdon in 2019* is wrong, and it has no signal word in it at all.
body.what_to_do: Ignore the signal words. Ask whether the stretch of time is finished. If it is, use the past simple, whatever words are in the sentence.

body.headline: Find the time expression. It decides the verb.

rows: present perfect, if it matters now

items.prompt: Which one is right? *The bridge reopened in May.* / *The bridge has reopened in May.*
items.why: *In May* is a closed time, so the verb has to be past simple.

items.prompt: Why is *Since April the waiting list grew by a third* wrong?
items.answer: *Since* opens a stretch that runs up to now, so the verb stays open: *has grown by a third*.
items.why: The time expression and the verb have to agree about whether the stretch is finished.
